procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Manipur at Imphal
procedural_history.impugned_order: Resolution of the Full Court (High Court) prescribing minimum marks for interview.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The petitioner(s) challenged the resolution of the Full Court (High Court) prescribing minimum marks for interview, arguing that it overrides statutory rules made under Article 234/309 and frustrates their legitimate expectation.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner(s) approached the Supreme Court via Writ Petition (Civil) No. 294 of 2015, challenging the High Court's decision. The Supreme Court considered whether the executive instructions in the form of the High Court's resolution could override statutory rules and whether the High Court's decision frustrated the petitioner's legitimate expectation.

directions: Parties to bear their own cost.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court’s decision frustrates the legitimate expectation of the petitioner?

facts: The recruitment process began under the unamended MJS Rules, 2005, which stipulated that the final merit list would be based on the aggregate marks from the written examination and the viva voce (interview).
The rules in place at the start of the process did not prescribe any minimum passing marks for the interview.
After the written examination was completed, and just before the interview, the High Court introduced a new requirement: a minimum of 40% marks in the viva voce to qualify.
This change was made through a High Court resolution, which is an executive instruction, not by amending the statutory rules.
The petitioner was not given any prior notice of this new requirement.
law: The Court relied on the doctrine of 'legitimate expectation'.

To establish a claim under this doctrine, a person must show: (i) the legitimacy of their expectation, and (ii) that the denial of this expectation led to a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution (the right to equality and fairness).
The principle of fairness requires public authorities to act in a predictable manner and honor their established practices and promises.
Executive instructions (like the High Court's resolution) cannot override statutory rules (like the MJS Rules, 2005).

A decision that frustrates a legitimate expectation must be justified by an overriding public interest and must meet the tests of fairness, consistency, and predictability to be valid under Article 14.
application: The Court determined that the unamended MJS Rules created a legitimate expectation for the petitioner that the selection would be based on the total combined marks of the written test and the interview.
The High Court's decision to introduce a minimum interview score after the recruitment process had already commenced frustrated this legitimate expectation.
The Court found this action to be a violation of Article 14 because it was unfair and unpredictable. The petitioner had no notice of the new rule and could not prepare accordingly.

Furthermore, the Court held that the High Court's resolution was illegal because, as an executive instruction, it could not override the existing statutory rules which specified the method for preparing the merit list.
The Court concluded that while the High Court's intention might have been bona fide, its action was not grounded in legality and failed the tests of fairness and predictability.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the High Court's decision to impose a minimum qualifying mark for the interview after the recruitment process had started did frustrate the petitioner's substantive legitimate expectation. This action was deemed illegal for overriding statutory rules and was found to be unfair, inconsistent, and unpredictable, thus violating Article 14 of the Constitution.

issue.issue_text: Whether such a course of action amounts to procedural fairness/unfairness?”

facts: A recruitment process was initiated under the Manipur Judicial Service Rules, 2005.
After the written test was completed, the Full Court of the High Court introduced a new requirement: a minimum cut-off of 40% for the viva-voce (interview).
This new rule was not communicated to the candidates, including the petitioner.
The petitioner passed the written exam but was disqualified for scoring less than the newly introduced 40% cut-off in the interview.
The petitioner was the sole Scheduled Caste (SC) candidate who had qualified in both the written exam and the interview based on the original rules.
law: The principle of legitimate expectation requires public authorities to act fairly, predictably, and honor established practices unless there is an overriding public interest to do otherwise.
Actions of the state must be fair, consistent, and predictable to comply with Article 14 of the Constitution (Right to Equality).
A candidate participating in a selection process does not waive their right to challenge an illegality or unconstitutional action within that process.
Procedural fairness requires that candidates are given notice of the rules and criteria by which they will be judged.
application: The Court determined that the petitioner had a 'substantive legitimate expectation' that the selection would be conducted according to the rules that were in place when the process began.
By introducing a minimum interview score after the written test was already over and without any prior notice, the High Court departed from the established procedure.
The Court found this action failed the tests of fairness, consistency, and predictability, as it changed the 'rules of the game' after it had started.
This unexpected and uncommunicated change was held to be a violation of the petitioner's legitimate expectation and, consequently, a violation of Article 14 of the Constitution.
The Court also noted that it was unjustified to deny the position to the sole SC candidate who had otherwise qualified under the existing rules.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's course of action—introducing a minimum cut-off mark for the interview after the selection process had commenced and without notifying the candidate—was procedurally unfair and violated the petitioner's legitimate expectation and Article 14 of the Constitution.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court’s decision frustrates the legitimate expectation of the petitioner?
appellant_arguments: The petitioner, having been declared successful in the written examination after a corrigendum was issued, had a legitimate expectation to be considered for the post based on the advertised rules.

The petitioner was initially wrongly declared to have failed the written exam and was only called for the interview after filing a Right to Information (RTI) Application to know his marks, which led to the High Court issuing a corrigendum.

The subsequent disqualification based on securing less than a minimum qualifying mark in the viva-voce, a criterion not stipulated in the Manipur Judicial Service Rules, 2005, frustrates the legitimate expectation created by his success in the written examination.
respondent_arguments: The counsel for the High Court relied on previous decisions of the Supreme Court during arguments.

arguments.issue_text: Whether such a course of action amounts to procedural fairness/unfairness?”
appellant_arguments: The course of action was procedurally unfair as the petitioner was initially declared unsuccessful in the written examination due to an error by the High Court.
It was only after the petitioner filed an RTI application that a corrigendum was issued declaring him successful, which demonstrates a lack of fairness in the initial evaluation process.

Imposing a minimum qualifying mark for the viva-voce, which was not mentioned in the advertisement or the relevant rules, amounts to changing the rules of the selection process after it had already commenced, which is procedurally unfair.
respondent_arguments: The counsel for the High Court relied on previous decisions of the Supreme Court during arguments.

cases.case_name: Sivanandan C.T. & Ors v. High Court of Kerala & Ors
cases.principle: The decision was considered squarely applicable to the facts of the case, implying reliance on the principle that new selection criteria (like minimum interview marks) cannot be introduced via administrative instructions after the selection process has commenced, if not provided for in the statutory rules.

cases.case_name: Dr.(Major) Meeta Sahai v. Union of India
cases.principle: A candidate participating in a selection process does not waive their right to challenge an illegality in it. A candidate's participation does not condone the misconstruction of statutory rules or discriminating consequences arising therefrom.

cases.case_name: Abhimeet Sinha v. High Court of Patna
cases.principle: In case of inconsistency between the recommendations of the Shetty Commission and the rules framed by the High Court, primacy should be given to the existing statutory rules.

cases.case_name: All India Judges Assn. v Union of India
cases.principle: Where statutory rules are silent regarding a specific matter (like prescription of minimum marks), administrative instructions can supplement the rules. However, administrative instructions cannot transgress a rule that makes a specific provision.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Executive instructions, recommendations, or resolutions cannot override existing statutory rules, particularly where those rules are categorical about a prescribed procedure.
obiter: A candidate's participation in a selection process does not condone any illegality within it, and such participation is necessary for the candidate to have the locus to challenge that illegality.
While statutory rules can be supplemented to fill in gaps, a High Court cannot act contrary to them.
In the absence of existing Rules, the High Court should follow the directions of the Supreme Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's decision to introduce a minimum 40% mark requirement for the interview after the recruitment process had already commenced, and in violation of the existing statutory rules, frustrated the petitioner's substantive legitimate expectation. This departure from the established procedure, without notice, fails the tests of fairness, consistency, and predictability, and is therefore arbitrary and violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.
legal_tests_applied: An individual who claims a benefit or entitlement based on the doctrine of legitimate expectation has to establish : (i) the legitimacy of the expectation; and (ii) that the denial of the legitimate expectation led to a violation of Article 14.
For a public authority to frustrate a claim of legitimate expectation, it must objectively demonstrate by placing relevant material before the court that its decision was in the public interest.
The decisions of public authorities must withstand the test of consistency, transparency, and predictability to avoid being regarded as arbitrary and therefore violative of Article 14.
why_appellant_lost: The decision to depart from the expected exercise of preparing the merit list as per the unamended Rules is clearly violative of the substantive legitimate expectation of the petitioners.
No notice was given to the petitioner regarding the imposition of minimum 40% marks for interview.
Prescribing minimum marks for viva voce... in the present case such a requirement was introduced only after commencement of the recruitment process and in violation of the statutory rules.
The decision... fails the tests of fairness, consistency, and predictability and hence is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India.
why_respondent_won: It would be unjustified to deny the sole SC candidate, who successfully qualified both the written exam and the interview, in accordance with the then existing rules.

A candidate by agreeing to participate in the selection process only accepts the prescribed procedure and not the illegality in it. In a situation where a candidate alleges misconstruction of statutory rules and discriminating consequences arising therefrom, the same cannot be condoned merely because a candidate has partaken in it.
policy_considerations: The principle of fairness in action requires that public authorities be held accountable for their representations, since the State has a profound impact on the lives of citizens.
Good administration requires public authorities to act in a predicable manner and honour the promises made or practices established unless there is a good reason not to do so.

The principles of good administration require that the decisions of public authorities must withstand the test of consistency, transparency, and predictability to avoid being regarded as arbitrary and therefore violative of Article 14.
State actions must be held to scrupulous standards to prevent misuse of public power and ensure fairness to citizens.
The constitutional scheme is sacrosanct and its violation in any manner is impermissible.
